title: The grid search
text: Each dot is the best score among the 96 combinations for that many inputs per split, one line per set of inputs. Lower is better. The gap between the lines is the cost of making the trees work out 'points still needed' for themselves; it is far bigger than anything the settings change.

title: How many trees are enough?
text: One tree alone is a poor, jumpy guesser. Averaging more trees smooths the answer, and the gain flattens after about 50. Adding trees never hurts accuracy, it only costs time. This is the same slider you can move on the Prediction tab.

title: ROC curve
text: Sweep the cutoff from strict to loose and track how many overs the forest catches against how many false alarms it raises, on the test seasons across a spread of totals. The closer the curve hugs the top-left corner the better. Area under it (AUC) is 0.81; a coin flip is 0.50.

title: Can you trust the percentages?
text: Test games are grouped by the chance the forest gave them. Dots on the dashed line mean 70% really did go over about 70% of the time. Each dot is about 357 game-and-total pairs from the test seasons.

title: Which inputs the model leans on
text: Shuffle one input so it carries no information and see how much worse the test predictions get. The thin line is the run-to-run noise. The inputs that say how many points are still needed carry the model; the rest add little.

title: What the cutoff changes
text: Calling 'over' at 50% is a choice. Raise the cutoff and the model calls over less often (gray falls) but those calls are right more often (blue rises), while its under calls get less reliable (orange falls). This is the cutoff slider on the Prediction tab, drawn across its whole range.
